paper_title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.

sections.content: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs Junhyeong Park1, Wook Jung1, Taeyoung Kim1, 2, Huiwon Jang1, 2 and Jinwoo Shin1, 2 1KAIST, 2RLWRLD Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in compatible representation, while decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests way for human demonstrations to serve as scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection. 1. Introduction Pretrained robotic policies, e.g., Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024), provide strong starting point for adapting general robotic capabilities to target deployment environment. However, major bottleneck remains in the collection of target robot demonstrations, as collecting such data on physical robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. It requires access to the physical platform, data collection pipeline (e.g., teleoperation), and repeated environment resets (Brohan et al., 2022; Khazatsky et al., 2024). Human demonstrations, in contrast, can be collected quickly and naturally without relying on dedicated teleoperation systems (Chi et al., 2024; Qiu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2023), using only lightweight camera setup. Yet, directly leveraging them to adapt robot policies remains challenging due to the substantial embodiment gap between humans and robots, particularly when the pretrained policy has been trained primarily on robot data. Prior works bridge human and robot demonstrations by placing them in common action space, either through latent actions inferred from frame transitions (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026; Bu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025) or through reconstructed world-space hand motion (Li et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2026; Hoque et al., 2026). While these approaches reduce the action-space mismatch across embodiments, they leave the perceptual gap largely unresolved. As result, VLAs must map distinct human and robot observations into shared action space, making reliable robot action prediction difficult. However, common action space alone does not make human demonstrations compatible with robot-pretrained VLA. Embodiment-dependent observations remain perceptually misaligned, while human and robot motions can still require different action realization dynamics. Our approach. Based on this insight, we introduce H2RB, training framework that incorporates human demonstrations into pretrained VLA policies without paired human-robot trajectories. First, geometryanchored alignment uses wrist-fingertip geometry to ground VLM output features across embodiments, without paired demonstrations or human-to-robot observation synthesis. Second, decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer shares action latents across embodiments while using separate decoders to avoid collapsing human and robot motion dynamics into single action mapping. Together, these components enable human-to-robot task transfer Correspondence to: Jinwoo Shin (jinwoos@kaist.ac.kr) Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs Figure 1: Human-to-robot task transfer with H2RB. H2RB transfers task experience from human videos to robots using pretrained VLAs by bridging the cross-embodiment perception and action gaps, without target-robot demonstrations or paired demonstrations. while facilitating learning from heterogeneous human-robot experience, as illustrated in Figure 1. We evaluate H2RB on two complementary forms of human-to-robot adaptation: within-skill object transfer and skill-level transfer. On OpenArm, where target behaviors are provided only through human demonstrations, H2RB improves object transfer from 8.0 to 51.8 and achieves skill-transfer score of 62.7, where shared-action co-training baselines fail. Heterogeneous human-robot training across multiple embodiments further improves these scores to 57.2 and 81.7, respectively. We additionally study robot-only downstream adaptation on RB-Y1, where cross-embodiment alignment improves success from 72% to 78% under matched heterogeneous training. Together, these results suggest that learning action-relevant representations from heterogeneous experience benefits both human-to-robot transfer and downstream robot adaptation. 2. Method H2RB bridges human-robot gaps through shared latent actions with embodiment-specific decoders and geometry-grounded VLM features, as illustrated in Figure 2. 2.1. Preliminaries: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models At timestep 𝑡, VLA predicts 𝐾-step action chunk A𝑡 := [a𝑡, a𝑡+1, . . . , a𝑡+𝐾1] from visual observation o𝑡, language instruction c, and the proprioceptive state s𝑡. Let h𝑡 denote the VLM conditioning tokens obtained from (o𝑡, c). Following flow-based VLAs (Bjorck et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026a), we use conditional flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022): for Gaussian noise 𝜖 𝒩 (0, I) and flow time 𝜏 [0, 1], we define A𝑡,𝜏 = (1 𝜏 )𝜖 + 𝜏 A𝑡 and optimize ℒFM = E[v𝜃(A𝑡,𝜏 , 𝜏 s𝑡, h𝑡) (A𝑡 𝜖)2]. Here v𝜃 is the velocity field predicted by the action expert. 2.2. Learning shared action space To reduce the action gap between human and robot demonstrations, we first express their motions in common physical parameterization. We then learn shared latent prediction space while retaining separate decoders for embodiment-dependent trajectory structure. Shared wrist-hand parameterization. For human videos, we first use HaWoR-based (Zhang et al., 2025a) reconstruction pipeline to recover wrist motion and hand articulation. We then transform the reconstructed motion into the robot coordinate convention and retarget it to the robot hand. We express human and robot actions in common wrist-hand representation (Kim et al., 2026b), i.e., a𝑡 = [p𝑡, r𝑡, q𝑡], where p𝑡 R3 is the wrist position, r𝑡 R6 is the 6D rotation representation, and q𝑡 R𝐷 is the hand configuration with 𝐷 joint angles for both human and robot demonstrations. At deployment, we convert the predicted wrist pose into robot arm motion via inverse kinematics. Decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer. shared wrist-hand parameterization does not eliminate source2 Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs (a) Decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer (b) Hand geometry-anchored alignment Figure 2: Overview of H2RB. (a) shared temporal encoder maps human and robot action chunks into common latent action space, while embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct actions for each domain. (b) Hand geometry-anchored alignment grounds VLA conditioning across embodiments, while the frozen encoder provides latent action targets. dependent action differences induced by distinct human and robot perceptions. We therefore learn shared latent action space while separating decoders for each embodiment to capture these differences. Specifically, given human actions A𝐻 in common wrist-hand representation, we train variational action autoencoder (Kingma and Welling, 2013) with shared encoder and embodiment-specific decoders (see Figure 2a). This encourages both sources to occupy compatible latent space while allowing each decoder to preserve source-specific trajectory structure. Geometry-anchored VLM conditioning Aligning actions alone does not resolve the human-robot perceptual gap, so we anchor VLM conditioning features to hand geometry shared across embodiments (Figure 2b). We ground VLM features using the current wrist pose and five wrist-local fingertip positions, denoted by g𝑡, obtained from reconstructed human motion or robot configurations. shared residual adapter 𝐴𝜑 and training-only readout 𝑅𝜔 produce hgeo )), where Pool denotes mean pooling over the VLM token sequence. We define ℒgeo as the masked Smooth-L1 loss between g𝑡 and g𝑡 over valid geometry coordinates. The action expert is conditioned on hgeo . (a) H2RB is trained jointly on human and robot demonstrations. (b) The trained policy executes target tasks introduced through human demonstrations, including object transfer on box, followed by skill transfer on opening. ℒVLA = ℒpred + 𝜆geoℒgeo. (2.2) where 𝜆geo weights the geometry objective. Implementation and optimization details are provided in Appendix A.3. The VLM backbone, tokenizer, and embodiment-specific decoders remain frozen during this stage. At deployment, numerical integration of the learned velocity field v𝜃 induces the latent-action policy 𝜋𝜃, conditioned on the robot observation, proprioceptive state, and instruction: 𝑡 𝜋𝜃( hgeo Zgen 𝑡 , s𝑡), Acmd 𝑡 = 𝐷𝐻 (Zgen 𝑡 ) (2.3) The decoder output is converted to robot commands using its prescribed inverse normalization and coordinate mapping. Both decoders reconstruct the same robot-compatible wrist-hand representation. Although deployment uses 𝐷𝐻 , the shared encoder and latent-action policy are learned from both human and robot demonstrations. 3. Experiments We evaluate H2RB in two stages. First, under controlled task-specific fine-tuning, we test whether human demonstrations transfer target objects and target skills to robot beyond vanilla human-robot co-training. Second, we test whether the same cross-embodiment principle remains useful when incorporated into heterogeneous multi-embodiment training. 3.1. Experimental setup Our real-world experiments use an OpenArm humanoid with Inspire hands, with all policies initialized from the robot-pretrained RLDX-1-IMG (Kim et al., 2026a); human demonstrations use the wrist-hand representation in Section 2.2. We compare matched co-training with separate embodiment-specific interfaces against HaWoR and Ego-Pi-based shared-action baselines, all without our geometry alignment or latent tokenizer and using the same adaptation data and training budget (see Tables 7 and 8). We study two axes of human-to-robot transfer. Object transfer introduces target objects through human pick-andplace demonstrations while retaining prior robot pick-and-place experience. Skill transfer introduces opening and closing interactions absent from the source robot demonstrations (see Figure 3). For these OpenArm tasks, we assign weighted task scores (0-100) based on execution progress, as detailed in Appendix B.2. For heterogeneous training evaluation, we additionally consider an RB-Y1 parcel-handling task, where the robot flips boxes and polybags to expose their shipping labels before pushing them onward (see Figure 4). RB-Y1 uses robot-only fine-tuning and binary success over 50 trials. 3.2. Human-to-robot task transfer Object transfer results. Table 1 summarizes transfer to objects introduced only through human demonstrations. In contrast, H2RB improves object transfer to 51.8 (+43.8) while retaining strong in-domain performance (49.0). Under object-placement shift, H2RB also outperforms Ego-Pi-shared action in both ID (30.2 to 55.0) and OOD (21.3 to 45.3) settings. These gains suggest that bridging the human-robot perceptual gap enables robust transfer to novel objects and locations while retaining robot-pretrained capabilities. Further breakdowns and geometry-grounding ablations are provided in Appendix C. Skill transfer results. Skill transfer exposes different bottleneck, as shown in Table 2. HaWoR-shared action fails to transfer Open/Close and degrades in-domain performance to 19.5, while Ego-Pi recovers in-domain execution to 70.5 but still achieves 0.0 on both target skills. This suggests that shared executable action space alone is insufficient for skill transfer; H2RB instead transfers both skills while further improving indomain performance from 0.0 to 81.0. This result highlights the importance of separating shared latent skill representation from embodiment-specific action realization when transferring behaviors across different motion distributions. Representative successful rollouts for each transfer task are shown in Figure 11. 3.3. Scaling to heterogeneous human-robot data We further adapt the pretrained VLA backbone through large-scale heterogeneous human-robot training (HT) across multiple embodiments, followed by downstream task-specific fine-tuning (FT). We evaluate its benefits in two downstream settings: human-to-robot transfer on OpenArm and robot-only adaptation on RB-Y1. Training details are provided in Appendix D. For OpenArm, heterogeneous training improves object transfer from 51.8 to 57.2 (+5.4) and skill transfer from 62.7 to 81.7 (+19.0), as shown in Figure 6. These gains demonstrate the benefit of additional heterogeneous training beyond task-specific co-training. For RB-Y1, parcel-orientation success improves from 64% with robot-only training to 72% with human-robot HT and 78% with geometry-grounded HT, as shown in Figure 5. 5 Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs Figure 4: RB-Y1 parcel-handling task. Box flipping (top) and polybag handling (bottom). Figure 5: Human-robot HT. Human-robot HT and geometry grounding improves robot-only downstream success. Figure 6: Effect of human-robot HT. HT improves transfer abilities, showing the scalability of H2RB. Figure 7: Instruction conditioning. Instruction conditioning improves skill transfer abilities. All variants use robot-only downstream FT without the shared action tokenizer, demonstrating the benefit of geometry grounding beyond human-to-robot task transfer. Together with the OpenArm results, it suggests that learning compatible action-relevant representations benefits downstream adaptation across different robots and task settings. 3.4. Enhancing skill transfer with instruction conditioning Separately from heterogeneous training, we examine whether stronger language conditioning can improve the transferred behavior for skill transfer. We treat the instruction as an explicit skill signal by concatenating its representation with the state-conditioned vision-language latent and re-injecting it throughout the expert layers. As shown in Figure 7, this improves skill transfer from 62.7 to 83.3 (+20.6), suggesting that sustained instruction access helps preserve task semantics during cross-embodiment execution. Implementation details are provided in Appendix A.4. 4. Analysis Human-to-robot transfer requires incorporating human-provided task structure while aligning cross-embodiment representations without discarding robot-specific execution dynamics. We analyze this separation through transfer failures, execution speed, and the resulting human-robot representation. 4.1. Qualitative analysis of transfer failures Human-only and robot-only policies exhibit complementary failure modes. Human-only policies capture the demonstrated interaction pattern but fail near contact due to inaccurate wrist alignment and grasp configuration (Figure 8a), whereas robot-only policies produce executable robot motions but fail to localize or reproduce behaviors absent from robot demonstrations (Figure 8b). Thus, human data provide the target behavior, while robot data provide embodiment-specific knowledge. (a) Fails to complete the grasp. (b) Unrelated to the target object location. (c) Fails to produce hand pose suitable for grasping. (d) Executes robot-observed pick-and-place motion in human-observed task environment. Combining the two sources in shared action format is still not fundamental solution. The shared-action baseline produces invalid grasp poses, indicating that coordinate-level alignment does not resolve the remaining perceptual mismatch (Figure 8c). Moreover, robot-conditioned predictions can remain closer to the robot latent distribution and revert to familiar robot behaviors even in human task deployment, such as pick-and-place instead of the human-demonstrated opening motion (Figure 8d). These failures motivate bridging the two domains beyond common physical action format. Accordingly, H2RB reduces the latent-level human-robot gap while retaining embodiment-specific decoders for source-appropriate action realization. 4.2. Cross-embodiment gap analysis Hand geometry-anchored alignment reduces the conditioning-space gap. Hand geometry-anchored alignment supervises human and robot observations through common hand-geometry target without requiring paired human-robot data. Compared with the Ego-Pi-shared action baseline, the PCA projection in Figure 9a shows that H2RB shifts robot conditioning features toward the human distribution, reducing the human-robot gap. This suggests that grounding VLM features in shared hand geometry makes the two embodiments more compatible in the conditioning space used for downstream action prediction. Decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer progressively aligns the prediction space. Table 3a shows that introducing the action tokenizer improves object transfer from 34.7 to 43.3 and enables skill transfer from 0.0 to 49.7. Cross-domain regularization further reduces the normalized human-robot latent gap (defined in Appendix A.5) from 3.81 to 1.53, 59.8% reduction, while improving object and skill transfer to 51.8 and 62.7, respectively. This alignment is particularly important at deployment, where robot-conditioned predictions can otherwise remain shifted toward the robot latent distribution, even for tasks learned from human data. The two-dimensional projections in Figure 9b provide qualitative view of this alignment, showing how cross-domain regression brings the human and robot latent distributions closer in the action latent space. Faster task execution from human data. Human demonstrations can provide faster task-specific motion while requiring substantially less collection time and robot interaction. To test whether these dynamics are preserved after transfer, we collected 100 robot teleoperation episodes for the same Open/Close tasks, with 50 episodes per task, and trained robot-only policy. (a) Vision-language conditioning features with hand geometry-anchored alignment alone (left) and H2RB (right). Arrows show adapter-induced displacements for the same observation. (b) Action-tokenizer latents without (left) and with (right) cross-domain latent regression, using per-tokenizer PCA. Human and II denote human tasks trained in within-skill object transfer and skill transfer, respectively. cm/s versus 2.52 cm/s for the robot-only policy, with comparable task performance (62.7 vs. 65.3). Because the embodiment-specific decoders preserve distinct action dynamics, the transferred policy can retain the faster motion from human demonstrations even when deployed on the robot. 5. Related Work Learning from human demonstrations. Human videos provide policy supervision through reconstructed or tracked hand motion (Zhang et al., 2025a; Hoque et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2022) or latent actions inferred from frame transitions (Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), supporting co-training and pretraining in works such as EgoMimic, EgoVLA, and EgoScale (Kareer et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Tao et al., 2025). Ego-Pi (Kim et al., 2026b) transfers task semantics through co-training in common wrist-hand space, while HumanEgo (Wang et al., 2026) learns from human demonstrations without robot data using hand-object representations. We focus on adapting robot-pretrained VLA to human-demonstrated target tasks while retaining experience from robot data. Cross-embodiment representation alignment. Human-data pretraining builds cross-embodiment priors (Yang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026), while explicit alignment relies on paired demonstrations (Xie et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026) or trajectory-based pseudo-pairs (Punamiya et al., 2025). PHANTOM and Masquerade instead synthesize robot-domain observations through inpainting and rendering (Lepert et al., 2025b,a). H2RB grounds pretrained VLA features in hand geometry independently for each observation, providing shared 8 Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs physical reference without paired data, trajectory matching, image synthesis, or prior human-robot backbone training. Latent action representations and decoding. Diffusion and flow-based policies generate continuous actions (Chi et al., 2025; Black et al., 2024; Ze et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), while latent diffusion separates generation from output reconstruction (Rombach et al., 2022; Peebles and Xie, 2023). LAD aligns retargeted action pairs (Bauer et al., 2025), and XL-VLA learns cross-hand latent representations (Jiang et al., 2026), both retaining embodiment-specific decoders for heterogeneous end-effectors. H2RB shares action latents across human-robot demonstrations while preserving source-specific motion dynamics through separate temporal decoders. 6. Conclusion We present H2RB, framework for adapting pretrained VLAs from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. Rather than relying on implicit cross-embodiment alignment, H2RB bridges perception through hand geometryanchored alignment and action through shared latent space with embodiment-specific decoders. Real-world experiments show improved object and skill transfer, further gains from heterogeneous training, and benefits for robot-only adaptation on different embodiment. These findings highlight the importance of learning reusable action-relevant structure from heterogeneous experience without enforcing identical action dynamics. We hope our approach helps bridge scalable human demonstration data and robot task adaptation, enabling pretrained VLAs to acquire new behaviors with human demonstration data. 9 Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs

Implementation details A.1. Action and geometry preprocessing Physical actions and current geometry. An OpenArm action concatenates three-dimensional wrist position, six-dimensional rotation representation, and six Inspire-hand coordinates, giving 15 values per timestep. Current hand geometry concatenates five wrist-local fingertip positions with the wrist pose, giving 24 values. These are different supervision targets: action learning uses future commanded wrist poses and hand coordinates, whereas hand geometry-anchored alignment uses the currently observed hand configuration. The bimanual wrist-hand representation concatenates the two hands to give 30-dimensional actions and 48-dimensional geometry. Before every action-expert block, the instruction slots are restored to their initial features, using the existing stream projection where required, while the other token representations evolve normally. Real-world data and evaluation For controlled human-to-robot transfer experiments, we use an OpenArm bimanual platform equipped with two Inspire RH56F1 dexterous hands. RB-Y1 evaluation examines robot-only downstream adaptation after heterogeneous training (Section D.4). The controlled transfer experiments use only the right arm and hand. head-mounted ZED 2i camera provides 1280 720 RGB observations from viewpoint approximately matching the human demonstrations. Policies receive one current right-camera RGB frame, language instruction, and 15-dimensional proprioceptive state comprising wrist position (3D), wrist rotation (6D), and hand joint angles (6D). Wrist poses are computed by forward kinematics in fixed canonical camera frame. Rollouts run at 20Hz. B.1. Training data and baseline definitions Transfer settings. Within-skill object transfer introduces Box, Ball, and Towel pick-and-place through human demonstrations while retaining source robot pick-and-place experience. Skill-level transfer introduces air-fryer opening and closing, which are absent from the source robot demonstrations. The corresponding robot indomain evaluation tasks are Doll PnP and Box PnP, respectively. Human and robot data are collected in the same environment, without frame-level human-robot correspondence. ID/OOD placement and rollout protocol For each target object, the object-transfer evaluation contains 20 in-distribution (ID) and 10 out-of-distribution (OOD) placement trials, totaling 90 target-task rollouts per policy. Skill transfer contains 15 Open and 15 Close trials, totaling 30. Robot in-domain performance is evaluated separately with 20 trials on the corresponding source task. Per-task evaluation counts are summarized in Table 10. Placement distribution and evaluation protocol. For object transfer, we divide the nominal workspace into four quadrants-right-upper (RU), right-lower (RD), left-upper (LU), and left-lower (LD)-and sample five initial object placements from each quadrant, yielding 20 in-distribution (ID) rollouts per object. Object orientation is randomized independently for each rollout. We use the same quadrant-based placement protocol during human data collection, such that the ID evaluation distribution follows the spatial support observed during training. For out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, we instead sample 10 initial placements outside these quadrants, while continuing to randomize object orientation. For skill transfer, the initial state of the air fryer is randomized by varying its degree of opening for both the Open and Close tasks. For skill transfer, Open and Close are each evaluated with 15 rollouts, so their reported average is equivalently the score pooled over all 30 target-task rollouts. We evaluate robot-only adaptation on the RB-Y1 bimanual platform, equipped with two 7-DoF arms and two 20-DoF Wuji Hand 2 dexterous hands, as shown in Figure 12a. head-mounted 22 Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs (a) RB-Y1 robot setup (b) Evaluation objects Figure 12: RB-Y1 experimental setup. (a) Bimanual robot platform. (b) Boxes and polybags used for parcel handling. ZED Mini stereo camera provides two RGB observations (left and right), each resized to 256 256. The policy receives both current RGB frames and 58-dimensional proprioceptive state comprising the left and right wrist poses (18D) and hand joint angles (40D). Each wrist pose consists of 3D position and 6D rotation representation. The policy predicts 58D absolute actions in the robot-base coordinate convention, with absolute joint-angle commands for both hands. Robot-only fine-tuning. All downstream policies are fine-tuned on the same robot-only dataset containing 726,752 frames after temporal retiming. The dataset and action targets are sampled at 30 Hz, with an action chunk length of 16 and 30k fine-tuning updates. We compare three HT variants initialized from the same pretrained backbone: robot-only HT, human-robot HT, and geometry-grounded human-robot HT. Robot-only HT uses the same training mixture with human demonstrations excluded, while the two human-robot variants differ only in geometry alignment. All variants use the same optimization settings for 200k HT updates and subsequently undergo robot-only downstream fine-tuning without the shared latent action tokenizer. Evaluation protocol. The task requires orienting parcels (Figure 12b), including boxes and polybags, such that their shipping labels face upward, and transferring them onto conveyor belt. We evaluate ten distinct objects with randomized initial orientations, repeating each object five times for total of 50 trials per policy. Success is binary: trial receives score of 1 only if the parcel is placed on the conveyor belt with its shipping label facing upward, and 0 otherwise. No intermediate subtask scores or partial progress credits are assigned.
